spark.summary: Four foundational algorithmic paradigms—Two Pointers, Fast & Slow Pointers, Sliding Window, and Dynamic Programming—that turn brute-force O(n^2) or O(2^n) searches into optimal O(n) or polynomial-time solutions.
spark.keyTakeaway: Identify the structural invariant first: monotonic sorted/array bounds call for Two Pointers or Sliding Window, cyclic state transitions call for Fast & Slow, and overlapping subproblems with optimal substructure call for Dynamic Programming.

concept.whyItMatters: Production bottlenecks—from rate limiters and stream deduplication to diff engines and knapsack resource schedulers—rely on these four patterns to keep latency O(n) and memory bounded under real-world scale.
whenToUse: Two Pointers / Sliding Window: Contiguous subarrays, sorted pair/triplet sums, streaming rate-limiters, and substring matching in O(n) time.
Fast & Slow Pointers: Linked-list cycle detection, finding midpoints in one pass, and O(1)-space duplicate/cycle detection in functional graphs.
Dynamic Programming: Optimization or counting problems (edit distance, Knapsack, LIS, scheduling) with overlapping subproblems.
whenNotToUse: Sliding Window when negative numbers break window monotonicity (use prefix sums + hash map instead).
Dynamic Programming when a greedy local choice is provably optimal (e.g., Dijkstra, Huffman coding, interval scheduling) or subproblems don't overlap.
Two Pointers on unsorted data where sorting (`O(n log n)`) destroys required original index order and a hash map gives `O(n)`.
keyPoints: **Two Pointers** eliminates a nested loop by moving `left` and `right` monotonically (`O(n)` time, `O(1)` space) on sorted arrays or partitioned buffers.
**Fast & Slow (Floyd's Cycle Detection)** advances `slow` by 1 and `fast` by 2; they are guaranteed to meet inside any cycle in `O(n)` time and `O(1)` space.
**Sliding Window** maintains a dynamic `[left, right]` invariant using a frequency map or monotonic deque, achieving `O(n)` amortized time because each pointer crosses each element at most once.
**Dynamic Programming** trades `O(n)` or `O(n * W)` memory for exponential speedup, and bottom-up tabulation often compresses 2D tables down to a `O(W)` 1D rolling array.
Recognizing which invariant holds (`monotonicity`, `cycle`, or `optimal substructure`) determines the optimal algorithm before writing a single line of code.

examples.title: API Gateway Sliding-Window Rate Limiter
examples.scenario: Checking a 60-second request cap per tenant by scanning a full timestamp log on every incoming request degraded to O(n) per call under 50k RPS bursts.
examples.outcome: Maintaining a Sliding Window deque (evicting timestamps `< now - 60s` from `left` while pushing `now` at `right`) reduced per-request amortized work to O(1) and kept gateway p99 overhead under 0.3 ms.

examples.title: Memory-Bounded Diff Engine with Space-Optimized DP
examples.scenario: Computing Levenshtein edit distance on two 20,000-line config files using a naive 2D `dp[m][n]` matrix allocated 1.6 GB of RAM and triggered OOMKills.
examples.outcome: Compressing the DP state to two 1D rolling rows (`O(min(m, n))` space) cut memory usage from 1.6 GB to 160 KB while preserving exact `O(m * n)` edit-distance accuracy.

tradeOffs.factor: Top-Down Memoization vs. Bottom-Up DP Tabulation
tradeOffs.pro: Top-down recursion is intuitive and computes only reachable subproblems.
tradeOffs.con: Bottom-up tabulation avoids recursion stack-overflow limits (`10^4+` depth) and enables `O(W)` 1D space compression.

tradeOffs.factor: Two Pointers (`O(n log n)` sort) vs. Hash Map (`O(n)`)
tradeOffs.pro: Sorting + Two Pointers uses `O(1)` auxiliary space and avoids hash-collision worst cases.
tradeOffs.con: A hash map achieves true `O(n)` time on unsorted inputs (e.g., 2-Sum) when `O(n)` RAM is acceptable.

tradeOffs.factor: Sliding Window vs. Prefix Sum + Hash Map
tradeOffs.pro: Sliding Window runs in `O(1)` extra space (for fixed alphabets) when all elements are non-negative.
tradeOffs.con: Negative numbers break shrink monotonicity, requiring Prefix Sum + Hash Map (`O(n)` space) for exact subarray sums.

failureModes.name: Sliding Window on Negative Weights
failureModes.description: Shrinking `left` when `window_sum > target` skips valid subarrays if later negative elements would have reduced the sum back to `target`.
failureModes.mitigation: Verify all values are non-negative (or the cost metric is monotonic) before using Sliding Window; otherwise use Prefix Sum + HashMap.

failureModes.name: Wrong Iteration Order in Space-Optimized DP
failureModes.description: Iterating `w` forward (`0..W`) instead of backward (`W..weight`) in 1D 0/1 Knapsack reuses the current item multiple times (turning it into Unbounded Knapsack).
failureModes.mitigation: Iterate capacity backward for 0/1 Knapsack (each item used at most once) and forward only for Unbounded Knapsack.

failureModes.name: Off-by-One Pointer & Base-Case Bugs
failureModes.description: Using `while left < right` vs `left <= right` or mis-initializing `dp[0]` silently drops single-element windows or empty-string base cases.
failureModes.mitigation: Explicitly test 0-element, 1-element, and all-identical-element edge cases before finalizing loop bounds.

failureModes.name: Recursion Stack Overflow in Memoized DP
failureModes.description: Deep top-down memoization (`n > 10,000` in Python/JVM) crashes with `RecursionError` or `StackOverflowError`.
failureModes.mitigation: Convert linear or grid recurrences to iterative bottom-up tabulation for production inputs.

commonMistakes: Applying Sliding Window to problems with negative numbers where shrinking the window is non-monotonic.
Forgetting to check `fast != null && fast.next != null` before advancing `fast = fast.next.next` in Floyd's cycle detection.
Confusing `0/1` Knapsack (reverse inner loop) with Unbounded Knapsack (forward inner loop) when using a 1D DP array.
Writing a `while` shrink condition inside Sliding Window that fails to update the auxiliary counter/map before incrementing `left`.
Jumping straight to DP without checking if a `O(n log n)` Greedy or Two Pointers invariant already solves the problem.

sections.content:
## The idea

Most brute-force sequence and optimization problems fail at scale because they re-examine identical ranges (`O(n^2)`) or recompute identical subproblems (`O(2^n)`). These four core patterns eliminate redundant work by exploiting structural invariants:

- **Two Pointers**: When data is sorted or partitioned, `left` and `right` move monotonically toward each other (or in the same direction), pruning `O(n^2)` pairs down to `O(n)`.
- **Fast & Slow Pointers**: Advancing a tortoise (`+1`) and hare (`+2`) detects cycles and finds midpoints in `O(n)` time and `O(1)` space without a visited `HashSet`.
- **Sliding Window**: Expands `right` to include new state and shrinks `left` only when an invariant breaks, keeping amortized cost `O(n)`.
- **Dynamic Programming (DP)**: Caches overlapping subproblem states (`dp[i]` or `dp[i][j]`) via memoization or bottom-up tabulation, turning exponential search trees into polynomial-time DAGs.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace **Minimum Window Substring** (Sliding Window) on `s = "ADOBECODEBANC"`, `t = "ABC"`:

1. **Setup**: Build `need = {'A': 1, 'B': 1, 'C': 1}` (`required = 3` unique chars). Initialize `left = 0`, `formed = 0`, `best = (inf, 0, 0)`.
2. **Expand `right`**: `right` advances from `0` to `5` (`"ADOBEC"`). Counts for `A`, `B`, `C` each hit `1`, so `formed == 3` (valid window of length 6).
3. **Shrink `left`**: While `formed == 3`, record `best` and increment `left`. Dropping `'A'` at index `0` drops `have['A']` below `need['A']`, setting `formed = 2` and halting the shrink at `left = 1`.
4. **Repeat to End**: `right` continues to `12`; each character is added by `right` once and removed by `left` at most once (`2 * 13 = 26` operations total), yielding the optimal `"BANC"` (length 4) in `O(|s| + |t|)` time.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Mathematical proofs and DP state compression
sections.content:
## Mathematical proofs and DP state compression

Why does **Floyd's Cycle Entry** algorithm work? Let the distance from head to cycle start be `a`, from cycle start to meeting point be `b`, and remaining cycle length be `c` (`L = b + c`). When `fast` and `slow` meet, `fast` has traveled `2(a + b) = a + b + k*L`, simplifying to `a + b = k*L`, or `a = (k - 1)L + c`. Resetting `slow` to `head` and advancing both by `+1` guarantees they collide at the exact cycle entry after `a` steps.

Similarly, in **Dynamic Programming**, recognizing state dependencies unlocks massive memory savings. In **0/1 Knapsack** (`dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], val[i] + dp[i-1][w - wt[i]])`), row `i` depends solely on row `i-1` at smaller weights. Replacing the 2D table with a single 1D `dp[w]` array and iterating `w` from `W` down to `wt[i]` preserves `dp[i-1][w - wt[i]]` intact before overwriting, cutting space from `O(n * W)` to `O(W)`.

## Pattern comparison matrix

| Pattern | Trigger Signal | Time Complexity | Space Complexity | Classic Examples |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Two Pointers** | Sorted array, pair/triplet sum, in-place partition | `O(n)` (or `O(n log n)` if sorting) | `O(1)` | 3Sum, Container With Most Water, Dutch National Flag |
| **Fast & Slow** | Linked list cycle, midpoint, `O(1)` duplicate search | `O(n)` | `O(1)` | Linked List Cycle II, Find Duplicate Number, Happy Number |
| **Sliding Window** | Contiguous subarray/substring, monotonic constraint | `O(n)` amortized | `O(1)` to `O(k)` | Min Window Substring, Longest Unique Substring, Rate Limiter |
| **Dynamic Programming** | Min/max cost, count ways, non-greedy choices | `O(n)` to `O(n * W)` | `O(W)` (compressed) | 0/1 Knapsack, Edit Distance, Coin Change, LIS (`O(n log n)`) |

## Failure modes

The most common bug in **Sliding Window** is applying it to subarrays with negative numbers (e.g., *Subarray Sum Equals K* with negative values), where shrinking `left` breaks monotonicity and misses valid solutions. In **DP**, iterating a 1D compressed array in the wrong direction silently converts 0/1 Knapsack into Unbounded Knapsack. Finally, **top-down memoization** on inputs exceeding `10^4` elements risks stack overflow in Python/Java unless converted to iterative bottom-up tabulation.

## Combining patterns in system problems

Real-world engineering problems frequently compose these patterns. For example, **Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS)** combines DP state definition (`tails[len]` = smallest ending element of an LIS of length `len + 1`) with binary search to drop `O(n^2)` DP to `O(n log n)`. Likewise, **Sliding Window Maximum** pairs a Sliding Window with a monotonic decreasing deque (`O(n)` time) to track real-time rolling p100 latency spikes without `O(n log k)` heap overhead.

## Practical checklist

- Check if the input is **sorted** or **monotonic** before reaching for a hash map or DP.
- Verify **non-negativity** before applying a shrinkable Sliding Window; switch to Prefix Sum + HashMap if negatives exist.
- Guard `fast != null && fast.next != null` on every iteration of Fast & Slow pointer loops.
- Write down the exact **DP state meaning**, **base case**, and **recurrence** before coding any loops.
- Convert deep top-down DP to **bottom-up tabulation** and compress 2D arrays to 1D rolling arrays where possible.
- Test boundary inputs: empty array, single element, all duplicates, and already-sorted/reverse-sorted sequences.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Deploy Core Algorithm Patterns: Two Pointers, Fast & Slow, Sliding Window & DP with strict monitoring thresholds and graceful degradation fallbacks.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Four foundational algorithmic paradigms—Two Pointers, Fast & Slow Pointers, Sliding Window, and Dynamic Programming—that turn brute-force O(n^2) or O(2^n) searches into optimal O(n) or polynomial-time solutions.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Fast & Slow Pointers applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Dynamic Programming.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Dynamic Programming experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Verify all values are non-negative (or the cost metric is monotonic) before using Sliding Window; otherwise use Prefix Sum + HashMap.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Identify the structural invariant first: monotonic sorted/array bounds call for Two Pointers or Sliding Window, cyclic state transitions call for Fast & Slow, and overlapping subproblems with optimal substructure call for Dynamic Programming.
Avoid trap: Applying Sliding Window to problems with negative numbers where shrinking the window is non-monotonic.
Avoid trap: Forgetting to check `fast != null && fast.next != null` before advancing `fast = fast.next.next` in Floyd's cycle detection.
When to reach for it: Two Pointers / Sliding Window: Contiguous subarrays, sorted pair/triplet sums, streaming rate-limiters, and substring matching in O(n) time.
When to reach for it: Fast & Slow Pointers: Linked-list cycle detection, finding midpoints in one pass, and O(1)-space duplicate/cycle detection in functional graphs.

putItTogether.title: Putting Core Algorithm Patterns Together
putItTogether.summary: Identify the structural invariant first: monotonic sorted/array bounds call for Two Pointers or Sliding Window, cyclic state transitions call for Fast & Slow, and overlapping subproblems with optimal substructure call for Dynamic Programming.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Core Algorithm Patterns before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Maintaining a Sliding Window deque (evicting timestamps `< now - 60s` from `left` while pushing `now` at `right`) reduced per-request amortized work to O(1) and kept gateway p99 overhead under 0.3 ms.
